value.name: Peacemaker Court
value.description: A division of the tribal courts providing a forum for traditional Alabama-Coushatta methods, customs and techniques to resolve disputes informally; peacemakers act as intermediaries and may not decide a matter the parties cannot resolve by agreement.
value.legal_basis: Comprehensive Codes of Justice, Title II – Peacemaker Code, Chapter I, Sec. 101-112
value.relationship_to_court: Established as a division of the courts under supervisory control of the Chief Judge of the Trial Division; a trial judge may refer a matter when all parties agree in writing, or parties may file a joint written request with the Clerk without filing a civil action. Tribal Probation may require a defendant to attend for traditional counseling as a probation condition.
value.enforcement: Agreements are presented as proposed consent decrees signed by the parties and approved by the trial court; the resulting judgment may be enforced like any other trial court judgment.

facts.note: Statements in peacemaking are confidential and inadmissible (Sec. 107); attorneys may not participate (Sec. 108); consent may be withdrawn at any time (Sec. 106(B)). Case types: any matter a judge believes suitable, criminal defendants with speedy-trial waiver, probation referrals.

value.title: Title II – Peacemaker Code
value.citation: Alabama-Coushatta Comprehensive Codes of Justice, Title II, Chapter I, Sec. 101-112
value.summary: Establishes the Peacemaker Court, peacemaker qualifications and role, referral routes, confidentiality, a bar on attorneys, and enforcement of agreements as consent judgments.

value.title: Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas Constitution and By Laws (listed by NARF alongside the Peacemaker Code)

facts.note: Listed by NARF; the constitution text was not reviewed for its specific peacemaking content.

value.name: Peacemaker Court of the Northern Arapaho Nation
value.description: A department of the Tribal Court intended to give formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Northern Arapaho methods of resolving disputes through mediation and traditional ways without judges or lawyers.
value.legal_basis: Northern Arapaho Code, Title 7. Peacemaker Code, Sections 101-702
value.relationship_to_court: Established as a department of the Tribal Court; a judge may appoint a peacemaker with the parties' concurrence, and civil or criminal cases may be transferred on stipulation or for good cause, with a stay of court proceedings that the court may lift on breach of a condition.
value.enforcement: Resolved disputes may be approved as judgments or orders of the Tribal Court and are enforceable; if all parties agree, a peacemaker may hear all sides and issue a decision that takes effect as a court judgment when entered, appealable under civil appeal rules.

facts.note: Listed matters (Sec. 104) include marital and family strife, parent-child disputes, minor neighbor disputes, alcohol use by family or neighbors, and minor community business transactions of $1,500 or less. Attorneys barred from proceedings (Sec. 106). Criminal transfers limited to cases without injury, with victim consent, or victimless offenses, or as a probation condition (Sec. 603-604). $10 fee for a judgment or protective order (Sec. 309).

value.title: Title 7. Peacemaker Code
value.summary: Establishes the Peacemaker Court, peacemaker powers and limits, request and transfer procedures, protective orders, and entry and enforcement of peacemaking judgments.

value.name: Peacemaker decision by consent of the parties
value.description: If parties agree in writing or orally, a peacemaker may hear all sides of a dispute and issue a decision.
value.legal_basis: Northern Arapaho Code, Title 7, Section 202(f)
value.relationship_to_court: The decision is submitted to the Tribal Court for entry as a written judgment.
value.enforcement: Takes the effect of a court judgment once entered; appealable under the Tribal Court's civil appeal rules.

facts.note: Kind recorded as arbitration because the code allows a binding decision by consent; the code itself calls it a peacemaker decision, not arbitration.

value.name: Chickasaw Nation Peacemaking Court
value.description: A division of the District Court operating under the customary and traditional law of the Nation, providing a forum for traditional Chickasaw methods of peacemaking to resolve disputes in a fair, informal and inexpensive manner.
value.legal_basis: Chickasaw Nation Code, Title 5, Chapter 14 (Peacemaking Court Act of 2003), Sections 5-1401.1 to 5-1401.17; Constitution Amendment V
value.relationship_to_court: Hears matters referred by the District Court with the agreement of the parties, on a written request, a joint motion, or the court's own motion with all parties' consent; unresolved matters return to the District Court, and matters under special domestic violence criminal jurisdiction are excluded.
value.enforcement: A signed written agreement and proposed dismissal order are reviewed and endorsed by the District Court as a final, non-appealable order, enforceable like other District Court orders.

own_term.name: Nanna alphi’sa ishtaa-asha ikbi
own_term.translation: Printed in parentheses under the chapter heading Chickasaw Nation Peacemaking Court; no separate gloss is given.

facts.note: Peacemakers are selected by the Supreme Court and kept on a roster; rules of civil and criminal procedure and evidence do not apply; counsel may not participate; statements are inadmissible; a 60-day limit before referral back. Peacemakers may use tribal cultural teachings and consult elders (Sec. 5-1401.5).

value.title: Peacemaking Court Act of 2003
value.citation: Chickasaw Nation Code, Title 5, Chapter 14, Sections 5-1401.1 to 5-1401.17
value.summary: Creates the Peacemaking Court within the District Court and sets peacemaker qualifications, referral procedures, form of agreements, enforcement and confidentiality.

value.name: Settlement conference (civil procedure)
value.description: In civil actions the court may order a settlement conference on its own motion or a party's request, presided over by a judge, court advocate or peacemaker; a judge may also assign a case on the pretrial docket to the Peacemaking Court.
value.legal_basis: Chickasaw Nation Code, Title 5, Section 5-202.22 (Pretrial Proceedings), subsections A and L
value.relationship_to_court: Part of the District Court's pretrial procedure.

value.title: Peacemaking: A Way of Life (presentation with Peacemaking Court forms, rules and procedures)

value.name: Chitimacha Peacemaker Court
value.description: Part of the Chitimacha Tribal Court System, intended to give formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional methods of resolving disputes through mediation, restorative justice and traditional ways.
value.legal_basis: Chitimacha Comprehensive Codes of Justice, Title I-A, Secs. 101-603
value.relationship_to_court: Supervised by the Chief Judge of the Tribal Court; a judge appoints a peacemaker on request, and civil or criminal cases may be transferred only with the written consent of all parties.
value.enforcement: Agreements may be presented as a draft judgment for the Tribal Court's approval; the resulting judgment is enforced like any other Tribal Court judgment.

facts.note: Listed matters include marital and family strife, extended family disputes, minor neighbor disputes, alcohol use, and minor community business transactions of $3,000 or less (Sec. 103). Attorneys barred except as witnesses or parties. Parties pay a reasonable sum set by the court for peacemaker compensation (Sec. 306). The court may have amended the title since 1990; the NARF copy shows the 1989-1990 dates.

value.name: Agreed arbitration by a peacemaker
value.description: Peacemakers may decide a disputed matter only if all parties agree in writing or before the Tribal Court.
value.legal_basis: Chitimacha Comprehensive Codes of Justice, Title I-A, Sec. 203 (Limitations; Peacemakers Not Judges; Agreed Arbitration)
value.relationship_to_court: The decision is entered by the Tribal Court.
value.enforcement: Has the effect of a court judgment when entered by the Tribal Court.

value.title: Title I-A – Peacemaker Court
value.citation: Chitimacha Comprehensive Codes of Justice, Title I-A
value.summary: Establishes the Peacemaker Court, its subject matter, peacemaker qualifications and powers, consent-based transfer, protective orders and enforcement of peacemaking judgments.

value.name: Peacemakers of the District Court (Choctaw Nation Peacemaking Act)
value.description: Peacemakers form a division of the District Court operating under the customs and traditions of the Choctaw people, providing a forum for traditional Choctaw methods of peacemaking to resolve disputes fairly, informally and inexpensively.
value.legal_basis: Choctaw Nation Peacemaking Act, Sections 1-11 and following
value.relationship_to_court: The District Court assigns and supervises peacemakers; matters come by written request, a party's motion for referral, a joint motion, or the court's own motion with all parties' consent, and unresolved matters return to the District Court.
value.enforcement: A signed agreement and proposed dismissal order are endorsed by the District Court and filed as a final, non-appealable order.

facts.note: Peacemakers must be familiar with Choctaw history, customs and traditions and may consult tribal elders (Sec. 3, 7). Attorneys may participate only at the peacemaker's discretion (Sec. 11(C)). as_of is the NARF posting year; enactment date not shown. Confidence high because the same file is published on the nation's own website (upload date used as as_of).

value.name: Peacegiving Court

own_term.name: Peacegiving
own_term.translation: English term used by the Tribes for their peacemaking forum; facilitators are called Peacegivers

value.description: A division of the Tribal Court providing a voluntary dispute resolution alternative grounded in tribal traditions of peace and healing, using restorative justice principles, traditional dispute resolution and mentoring; also supervises Child in Need of Supervision matters.
value.legal_basis: Tribal Code Chapter 2-14 (Ordinance No. 072), Sections 2-14-1 to 2-14-19
value.relationship_to_court: Subject to supervision of the Chief Judge; the Tribal Court may transfer any case with the consent of all parties (or of the child in Child in Need of Supervision or juvenile offender matters).
value.enforcement: Agreements must be written and fully executed and have no legal force until approved by the Tribal Court; breaches of confidentiality may be punished as contempt.

facts.note: Peacegivers may accept gifts of nominal value after the case ends, described in the code as in the tradition of potlatch (2-14-12). Ordinance states it does not waive sovereign immunity (2-14-18).

value.title: Chapter 2-14 – Peacegiving Court
value.citation: CTCLUSI Tribal Code, Title 2 – Rules of Procedure, Chapter 2-14
value.summary: Establishes the Peacegiving Court, peacegiver qualifications, consent-based transfer, confidentiality, and court approval of agreements.

value.title: Chapter 2-13 – Wellness Court Rules
value.citation: CTCLUSI Tribal Code, Title 2 – Rules of Procedure, Chapter 2-13
value.summary: Per NARF, provides procedures, purposes, policies and sanctions for a Wellness Court that diverts offenders with substance abuse issues from mainstream courts.

facts.note: Summary from NARF's description; listed among NARF's youth and family peacemaking laws.

value.name: Peacegiving Program

own_term.name: Peacegiving
own_term.translation: English term used by the Tribe; facilitators are called Peacegivers

value.description: A program under supervision of the Chief Judge in which Peacegivers resolve disputes using restorative justice principles and traditional Tribal dispute resolution and community integration values and practices.
value.legal_basis: Coquille Tribal Ordinance Chapter 655 (Peacegiving Procedures), 655.010-655.900
value.relationship_to_court: With the parties' consent the Tribal Court may transfer any case or dispute; the code also provides that cases involving a juvenile party may be transferred with or without consent.
value.enforcement: Agreements must be in writing and have no legal force until approved by the Tribal Court; confidentiality breaches may be treated as contempt.

facts.note: Section 655.110(2) as printed names the Tribal Council as the body that may transfer juvenile cases without consent. Ordinance states it does not waive sovereign immunity (655.800).

value.title: Chapter 655 – Peacegiving
value.summary: Establishes the Peacegiving program, Peacegiver qualifications and duties, transfer of cases, confidentiality and court approval of agreements.

value.name: Siletz Community Law Court

own_term.name: Gwe-shvt-naga
own_term.translation: in between he, she, or it walks (title for the peacemaker)

value.description: Part of the Tribal Court system giving formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Siletz methods of resolving disputes through mediation and traditional ways; peacemakers are titled Gwe-shvt-naga.
value.legal_basis: Siletz Tribal Code § 3.300 and following (Siletz Community Law Court)
value.relationship_to_court: The Community Law Court Judge supervises the peacemakers; civil and criminal actions may be transferred from Tribal Court where all parties consent in writing.
value.enforcement: Judgments may be enforced as any Tribal Court judgment; they may not be appealed, but a party may move to modify for a $30 fee.

facts.note: Language of the term is not named in the source, so language_tag is 'und'. Listed matters include marital disputes and family strife, extended family disputes, minor neighbor disputes, alcohol use, and minor community business transactions of $2,500 or less. Peacemakers must be enrolled Siletz members certified by Tribal Council. Attorneys barred. Updated from the 2005 version on NARF (peacemaking.narf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Siletz-Comm-Law-Court-09-16-2005.pdf); the 2005 text said the court was not yet authorized for divorce, separation or annulment, and that sentence does not appear in the 2025 text read.

value.name: Agreed arbitration by Gwe-shvt-naga/Peacemaker
value.description: Peacemakers may decide a disputed matter only if all parties agree in writing or before the Tribal Court.
value.legal_basis: Siletz Tribal Code § 3.305 (Limitations; Gwe-shvt-naga/Peacemakers Not Judges; Agreed Arbitration)
value.relationship_to_court: Decision is entered by the Siletz Community Law Court Judge.
value.enforcement: Has the effect of a court judgment when entered.

value.title: Siletz Community Law Court
value.summary: Establishes the Community Law Court and Gwe-shvt-naga/Peacemakers, subject matter, consent-based transfer, judgments and their enforcement.

value.name: Peacemaker conference (Peace Making Roster)
value.description: An optional, consent-based way of resolving disputes in which a peacemaker from a roster of tribal members mediates before or instead of trial; peacemakers conduct informal conferences and encourage an agreement acceptable to all parties.
value.legal_basis: Hopland Tribal Code, Title 12, Chapter 12-1, Sections 12-1.20.020 and 12-1.100.010 to 12-1.100.070
value.relationship_to_court: Parties file a request with the Court Clerk and the judge refers the case to a rostered peacemaker if no party objects; no lawsuit need be pending, and parties may continue in Tribal Court if peacemaking fails.
value.enforcement: A written settlement signed by the parties and the peacemaker is an enforceable agreement; if a lawsuit is pending it is filed and treated as the final judgment.

facts.note: Roster kept by Tribal Council with advice of the Chief Judge and Culture Committee; peacemakers must be tribal members at least 50 years old. Counsel not allowed; a party may have a Big Talker (a non-lawyer tribal member or relative) only as needed to understand the proceedings. Discussions are confidential. as_of is NARF posting year.

value.title: Tribal Court Ordinance – Peacemakers
value.citation: Hopland Tribal Code, Title 12, Chapter 12-1, Section 12-1.100
value.summary: Creates a Peacemaker roster and sets qualifications, duties, request procedure, representation rules and enforceability of settlements.

value.title: Validity and Enforceability of Arbitration Agreements
value.citation: Hopland Tribal Code, Title 12, Chapter 12-3 (Ordinance No. 02-17-07)
value.summary: Gives the Tribal Court authority to determine validity of arbitration agreements, compel or enjoin arbitration, appoint arbitrators, and confirm, correct or vacate awards.

value.name: Presentation of claims to Tribal Council (Tribal Claims Ordinance)
value.description: Claims for money or damages against the Tribe or its business enterprises, including employee wage claims, must be presented to and acted on by the Tribal Council before suit.
value.legal_basis: Hopland Tribal Code, Title 12, Chapter 12-4, Sections 12-4.10 to 12-4.150
value.relationship_to_court: A prerequisite to filing suit.

value.name: Traditional Peacemakers Panel
value.description: A panel named in the civil actions chapter that may allow alternative service, decides tolling questions, and in execution of judgments orders the judgment debtor to appear, determines available property and orders seizure.
value.legal_basis: Kalispel Law and Order Code, Chapter 3 – Civil Actions, Sections 3-1, 3-5.01, 3-21 (Execution of Judgments)
value.relationship_to_court: Functions within the Tribal Court's civil process as described in Chapter 3.
value.enforcement: Orders seizure and public sale of a judgment debtor's property; failure to appear may be deemed contempt.

facts.note: Kind 'other' because the chapter shows the panel acting in an adjudicative and enforcement role rather than as a consensual forum; the chapter reviewed does not define the panel's composition.

value.title: Execution of Judgments (Traditional Peacemakers Panel)
value.citation: Kalispel Law and Order Code, Chapter 3, Sec. 3-21
value.summary: Authorizes the Traditional Peacemakers Panel to examine judgment debtors and order seizure and sale of property, with a hardship exemption and redemption period.

value.name: Peacemaker Mediation Forum
value.description: A nonadversarial forum within the Tribal Court structure for resolving disputes between Tribal members and others within the Tribe's jurisdiction; guidelines are to reflect the Tribe's historical traditions and modern methods of dispute resolution.
value.legal_basis: Karuk Tribal Code, Section 3.05.100 (Res. 10-R-111 § 10.9)
value.relationship_to_court: When a petition is filed with the Clerk, the forum is used before proceeding to a formal court hearing; parties may continue in court if mediation fails.

facts.note: Participation recorded as 'required' because the code says the forum shall be used before a formal hearing once a petition is filed.

value.title: Peacemaker Mediation Forum
value.summary: Establishes the Peacemaker Mediation Forum as a step before formal court hearings and directs the court to create forum guidelines.

value.name: Peacemaker System
value.description: Part of the Tribal Court System but independent from Tribal Court judges, providing formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Kickapoo methods of resolving disputes through mediation and traditional ways; Kickapoo customs and traditions are its guiding principles.
value.legal_basis: Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas Code, Chapter 4 – The Peacemaker System, Sections 4.1-4.64; Chapter 1, Sec. 1.7
value.relationship_to_court: Any individual may request peacemaking through the court or by contacting a certified peacemaker directly; civil or criminal actions may be referred where all parties agree, and the Tribal Court may require peacemaking as a probation condition. The system cannot compel attendance.
value.enforcement: A Tribal Court judgment on Peacemaker System proceedings may be enforced as any other Tribal Court judgment; peacemakers may decide a matter only with all parties' written consent, and such a decision takes effect as a court judgment when entered.

facts.note: Peacemakers must be Kickapoo members over 25, certified by the Traditional Council; attorneys may not serve or participate. Each party pays $20 toward peacemaker compensation. Peacemakers may also serve entities other than the Tribal Court (Sec. 4.3(D)). as_of is NARF posting year.

value.title: Chapter 4 – The Peacemaker System
value.citation: Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas Code, Chapter 4; Chapter 1, Sec. 1.7
value.summary: Establishes the Peacemaker System, peacemaker qualifications and certification by the Traditional Council, procedures, protective orders, complaints and transfers from Tribal Court.

value.name: Mnodaawin

own_term.name: Mnodaawin
own_term.translation: Odawa peacemaking (as glossed in the rule)

value.description: The Odawa peacemaking program to which Tribal Court cases may be transferred.
value.legal_basis: Little Traverse Bay Bands Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule XXIX (Mnodaawin)
value.relationship_to_court: A party may request transfer of a Tribal Court case at any time on evidence that all parties voluntarily consent and the Mnodaawin program has affirmed it can accept the case.
value.enforcement: Parties must consent to be bound by any agreement reached in Mnodaawin.

facts.note: Language tag otw (Ottawa/Odawa) assigned because the rule glosses the term as Odawa peacemaking.

value.title: Rule XXIX: Mnodaawin
value.citation: Little Traverse Bay Bands Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule XXIX
value.summary: Allows a party to request transfer of a Tribal Court case to Mnodaawin on all parties' voluntary consent to participate and be bound and the program's acceptance.

value.name: Navajo Nation Peacemaking Program

own_term.name: Hózhóójí Naat’áanii
own_term.translation: Peacemaking Program (the statutory program name; the Judicial Branch uses hózhóójí naat’áanii for the Peacemaker)

value.description: A program within the Judicial Branch serving as the central point of peacemaking information and coordination; it promotes a non-adversarial forum where parties voluntarily agree or are referred to peacemaking, peacemaking counseling for court clients, sentencing recommendations on request, and education on Navajo culture and traditions.
value.legal_basis: 7 N.N.C. §§ 409-413 (Chapter 3, Subchapter 10, Navajo Nation Peacemaking Program)
value.relationship_to_court: Located in the Judicial Branch under the legislative oversight of the Judiciary Committee and a Plan of Operation; per the Plan of Operations, where a court order is sought the matter must first be filed in court and then referred to peacemaking by the court.
value.enforcement: Not specified in the subchapter reviewed.

facts.locator: 7 N.N.C. §§ 409-413; Title 7 annotation citing In the Matter of the Estate of Kindle (Nav. Sup. Ct. 2001)
facts.note: own_term spelling taken from NARF's Tribal Peacemaking Laws page ('Hózhóójí Naat’áanii'); the Navajo Nation Code PDF text layer shows 'Hózh==jí Naat'áanii' and the Judicial Branch plan page shows 'hózh̨ǫ́ójí naat’áanii' (font conversion artifacts in both). A Code annotation states local peacemaking programs exist in the seven judicial districts and are also used for probate. Child-welfare and juvenile case types are from the Plan of Operations (family preservation and reunification; Álchíní Bi Beehaz’áannii Act matters).

value.name: Diné Traditional Peacemaking

own_term.name: hózh̨óji naat’aah
own_term.translation: Diné traditional peacemaking (as glossed by the Judicial Branch)

value.description: One of several traditional services available through the Peacemaking Program; the Plan of Operations names four kinds of participants (the peacemaker, the decision-making parties called naałchidí, contributing family members and others called atah naaldeehí, and silent observers) and refers to peacemaking principles drawn from the Fundamental Law.
value.legal_basis: Peacemaking Program Plan of Operations, Part I (adopted under 7 N.N.C. § 413)
value.relationship_to_court: May not be initiated in the Program for a dispute in which a court order is sought; such matters are filed in court first and referred by the court for all or part of the dispute.
value.enforcement: The Plan describes finality as established by the participants' agreement; court effect is not described on this page.

facts.note: Terms copied as displayed on the Judicial Branch page, which uses a legacy Navajo font conversion. A set peacemaker fee called yeel is paid to community-based peacemakers through the Program; the Program may pay it for indigent participants in family preservation and reunification matters and in children's code matters. The page also describes ceremonial elements the Nation has chosen to publish; they are not summarized here. Undated page; as_of is the access date.

value.title: Subchapter 10. Navajo Nation Peacemaking Program
value.summary: Recognizes the Peacemaking Program within the Judicial Branch, sets its purposes and authority to conform procedures to traditional concepts including K'é and clanship, and places it under Judiciary Committee oversight and a Plan of Operation.

value.title: Peacemaking Program Plan of Operations
Form 1 Peacemaking Referral Form

facts.note: Seen in search results only; not opened.

value.title: Peacemaking Program Brochure OCT.2025

facts.note: Seen in search results only; download failed.

value.title: Peacemaking Program Plan of Operation (2013 copy hosted by Tribal Justice)

facts.note: Seen in search results only; not opened. Title inferred from file name and result title 'PPPO2013 2 25'.

value.name: Peacemakers (Peacemakers Council)
value.description: A forum of Elders and other Tribal Members who volunteer as mediators for disputes arising on Tribal Lands; Peacemakers act by consensus decision, do not decide fault or liability and cannot coerce an agreement.
value.legal_basis: 1 M.P.T.L. ch. 4, §§ 1-11 (originally established by TCR102693-01)
value.relationship_to_court: Parties must consent in writing; matters may come by direct mediation request, by resolution of the Tribal Council or Elders Council, or by referral from the Tribal Court or the Mashantucket Employment Rights Office with both parties' consent. Excluded: appeals from Council, Elders Council or court decisions (unless specifically referred), grievances, vendor contract disputes with the Tribe, and appeals from certain committees and programs.
value.enforcement: Parties sign a written Agreement acknowledging it may be enforced in Tribal Court; an action to enforce a referred agreement must be filed within thirty days of the breach becoming known.

facts.note: Proceedings are confidential and participants sign non-disclosure agreements (§ 6). Filing a mediation request stays limitation periods for administrative or court actions (§ 10).

value.title: Chapter 4 – Peacemakers
value.summary: Defines the Peacemakers' mediation jurisdiction, membership, confidentiality, referral and mediation procedure, and court enforcement of signed agreements.

value.name: Peacemaker Court
value.description: A vehicle for parties to reach consensual solutions by talking things out, described by the Tribe as the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribal way of resolving conflicts, predating the court system; it need not determine fault.
value.legal_basis: Chapter 3: Operation of Peacemaker Court, Sections 1-3 and following
value.relationship_to_court: The Chief Judge appoints peacemakers (two, one male and one female) for civil matters within District Court jurisdiction; peacemaking is not allowed in criminal matters, and peacemakers report results to the District Court or Chief Judge.
value.enforcement: An agreement reached by the parties is reduced to writing, signed, and is a final decision without appeal.

facts.note: Eligible matters include family and other relationships, community relations among neighbors, and civil matters involving personal, community or economic relationships. Parties are asked to participate without attorneys. Peacemakers may involve service providers including traditional healers and leaders, with consent. The Tribe's own pages link a brochure, a participant's guide and an intake form; see the material facts. as_of is NARF posting year.

value.name: Choctaw Itti-kāna-ikbi Court (Choctaw Peacemaker Court)

own_term.name: Itti-kāna-ikbi
own_term.translation: peacemaker (the code uses the term for the Choctaw Peacemaker Court and its peacemakers; spelling fixed by Tribal Council Resolution 42-81(A))

value.description: A division of the Tribal Court providing a forum for traditional Choctaw methods of peacemaking to resolve disputes fairly, informally and inexpensively, supervised by the Senior Itti-kāna-ikbi.
value.legal_basis: Choctaw Tribal Code, Title XXIV, Chapter 1, §§ 24-1-1 to 24-1-17
value.relationship_to_court: Has original jurisdiction over cases filed by joint petition of all parties and over matters referred by the Choctaw Criminal, Civil or Youth Court; a referred case moves to the Itti-kāna-ikbi Court's docket and returns to the referring court if no agreed resolution is possible.
value.enforcement: A signed agreement and proposed dismissal order are reviewed by the Itti-kāna-ikbi Judge and entered; the code provides for enforcement of judgments (§ 24-1-12). The court may compel attendance and seek contempt.

facts.note: Peacemakers on the roster are called Itti-kāna-ikbi aliha (as printed); they are selected from the Choctaw community and approved by the Tribal Council. Case types reflect referral from criminal, civil and youth courts. Language tag cho (Choctaw). as_of is NARF posting year. Confidence high because the same file is published on the nation's own website (upload date used as as_of).

value.title: Title XXIV – Choctaw Peacemaker Code (Choctaw Itti-kāna-ikbi Code)
value.citation: Choctaw Tribal Code, Title XXIV, Chapter 1
value.summary: Creates the Itti-kāna-ikbi Court, sets its jurisdiction, peacemaker roster, use of tribal traditions, procedures, form and enforcement of agreements.

facts.note: Confidence high because the same file is published on the nation's own website (upload date used as as_of).

value.name: Peacemaker Court
value.description: A voluntary forum, sitting as a panel of three Peacemakers, for traditional, non-adversarial Nez Perce methods of dispute and conflict resolution as an alternative to the Tribal Court, specialty courts and court-imposed sanctions; it does not ascribe fault and uses dialogue to reach consensus-based solutions.
value.legal_basis: Nez Perce Tribal Code §§ 1-8-1 to 1-8-11
value.relationship_to_court: Hears matters on order of a Tribal Court judge or specialty court official: adult criminal matters excluding listed serious and violent offenses, any juvenile delinquency matter, and civil matters other than contract disputes where all parties agree; in criminal and juvenile matters the prosecutor, defendant and victim must agree. Peacemakers report regularly to the referring court.
value.enforcement: Agreements may be confirmed as a Tribal Court or specialty court judgment or order and enforced like other orders; agreements from minor disputes heard at the parties' own request outside court are not enforceable in court.

facts.note: The code provides that peacemakers may suggest participation in Nez Perce activities and practices, naming as examples sweat lodge ceremonies, traditional drumming or dancing, and instruction in the Nimiipuu language. Peacemakers are unpaid volunteers unless a program funds a stipend. The court's guidelines are set out in a Peacemaker Court Handbook (§ 1-8-7).

value.name: Peacemaking and Mediation Division of the Trial Court (peacemaking)
value.description: A division of the Trial Court providing peacemaking at all stages of litigation, including appeals, by peacemakers recognized either by the Nation's Cultural Heritage Department or by the Trial Court, as the parties choose; the law states culturally sensitive information may be omitted from the procedural rules.
value.legal_basis: 8 O.C. 801.6 (Peacemaking and Mediation Division); 7 O.C. 702.6; 7 O.C. 705.7
value.relationship_to_court: Judges must inform parties in every case of peacemaking and mediation and may refer parties who agree to attend, except where attendance would cause undue hardship or endanger a party; the court bears the cost of referred sessions.
value.enforcement: A written agreement certified by the peacemaker is submitted to the judge and included in the order as a stipulation; violation of the resulting order is punishable as contempt.

facts.note: Peacemakers may not act in contempt matters or issue process. Proceedings are closed to the public (801.4-4). as_of is NARF posting year.

value.name: Peacemaking and Mediation Division of the Trial Court (mediation)
value.description: Mediation provided by persons or entities recognized and contracted by the Trial Court; each mediator must have at least 25 hours of mediation training or 3 years of dispute resolution experience, and in divorce matters training on domestic violence.
value.relationship_to_court: Available at all stages of litigation on court referral with the parties' agreement; parties may instead use a private mediator at their own expense after filing notice with the clerk.
value.enforcement: Agreement is written, reviewed by counsel if any, certified by the mediator, and included in the court's order as a stipulation; violation is punishable as contempt.

value.title: Peacemaking and Mediation Division
value.summary: Establishes the Peacemaking and Mediation Division of the Trial Court, referral rules, peacemaker and mediator standards, and entry of agreements as stipulated orders.

value.title: Divorce, Annulment, Legal Separation – Peacemaking and Mediation
value.summary: Allows referral of divorce, annulment and legal separation parties to peacemaking or mediation with their agreement, with a domestic abuse screen and mediator training requirements.

value.title: Child Custody, Placement and Visitation – Peacemaking and Mediation

facts.note: Section heading confirmed; contents not reviewed in detail. NARF summarizes 702.6 and 705.7 together as providing authorization, procedures, appeals policies and referral standards.

value.name: Application to serve as Peacemaker/Mediator (background check and interview process)

facts.note: Rule 1.10 governs applications from prospective peacemakers and mediators outside the Judiciary (application, background check, interview). It is a qualification process rather than a training course.

value.name: Peacemaker Court of the Oneida Indian Nation (Peacemakers division of the Trial Court)
value.description: The Trial Court includes a Peacemakers division; peacemaking is to be encouraged in all cases and is governed by the Peacemaking Rules in effect from time to time. Peacemakers are persons with experience in peacemaking, arbitration or mediation. The Peacemaking Rules establish the Peacemaker Court as part of the Nation Court System to give formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Oneida Indian Nation methods of resolving disputes; peacemaking uses Nation religious or other traditional ways of mediation and problem-solving.
value.legal_basis: Oneida Indian Nation Ordinance O-97-02, preamble, Article 8 (Peacemaking) and Article 12(1)(g); Oneida Indian Nation Peacemaking Rules 1-18
value.relationship_to_court: The Chief Judge of the Trial Court appoints a peacemaker in any matter deemed appropriate or where a party requests peacemaking.
value.enforcement: Peacemakers may decide a matter only if all parties agree in writing, and such a decision has the effect of a court judgment when entered by the Nation Court; peacemakers may request contempt for persons who ignore subpoenas.

facts.note: Peacemaking Rules read from OCR of a scanned copy dated 5/1/97 (source oneida-indian-nation-peacemaking-rules-1997); attorneys are barred unless witnesses or parties (Rule 3). The ordinance also refers to a Claims Commission established by Ordinance O-94-02A.

value.title: Ordinance O-97-02, Article 8 – Peacemaking
value.citation: Oneida Indian Nation Ordinance O-97-02, Art. 8
value.summary: Directs that peacemaking be encouraged in all cases before the Oneida Nation Court under the Peacemaking Rules.

value.title: Oneida Indian Nation Peacemaking Rules

value.name: Peacemakers Circle
value.description: A separate mediating branch established in the constitution's Dispute Resolution System; peacemakers are selected by the Nation's members at a General Council meeting and are responsible for mediating disputes voluntarily submitted by the parties.
value.legal_basis: Constitution of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, Article VI (Dispute Resolution System), Sections 1-3
value.relationship_to_court: Established alongside, and separate from, the Judicial Council (District Court, Court of Appeals and Employment Disputes Tribunal); procedures are to be defined by Nation law.

facts.note: NARF's summary adds that the provision covers foreclosure of further District Court proceedings and an attorney ban; those details were not located in the Article VI text reviewed and may be in implementing law.

value.name: Employment Disputes Tribunal
value.description: A five-magistrate tribunal within the Judicial Council responsible for deciding all government employment related disputes; two magistrates are appointed by the Tribal Council, two by the Nation's employees, and one by the other four.
value.legal_basis: Constitution of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, Article VI, Sections 1-3
value.relationship_to_court: Part of the Judicial Council; the District Court's powers exclude government employment related disputes, which go to the Tribunal.

facts.note: Coined kind 'employment-tribunal': an adjudicative forum with jointly appointed members, not a consensual process.

value.title: Article VI – Dispute Resolution System
value.citation: Constitution of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, Art. VI
value.summary: Establishes the Judicial Council (District Court, Court of Appeals, Employment Disputes Tribunal) and a separate Peacemakers Circle to mediate disputes voluntarily submitted.

value.name: Tribal traditional peacemaking forum (Traditional Peacekeeping)
value.description: On the Tribal Court's recommendation, a case involving a class D offense may be referred to a tribal traditional peacemaking forum for adjudication.
value.legal_basis: Skokomish Tribal Code 9.11.030 (Traditional Peacekeeping)
value.relationship_to_court: The forum submits a case report to the Tribal Court and all parties detailing action taken, restrictions and conditions.
value.enforcement: Failure to comply with requirements in the case report may be treated as a violation of a court order.

facts.note: Sentencing policy (9.11.010) favors restitution to the victim and community.

value.title: Traditional Peacekeeping
value.summary: Allows referral of class D offense cases to a tribal traditional peacemaking forum, whose case report conditions are enforceable as court orders.

value.name: Traditional Peacemaking Court
value.description: A branch of the Tribal Court giving formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Chippewa methods of resolving disputes through mediation and traditional ways; composed of one or more Tribal Judges serving separately as Peacemakers, who must certify training in peacemaking or mediation.
value.legal_basis: Sokaogon Chippewa Community Code, Chapter 1, Sections 1.1.8 to 1.1.12
value.relationship_to_court: Has original jurisdiction when all parties agree and request peacemaking, and over juvenile delinquency and educational neglect cases as provided in other codes; judges may refer civil or criminal cases where all parties agree, except hunting and fishing, traffic, and Children in Need of Protective Services cases. The Tribal Court keeps jurisdiction over referred cases.
value.enforcement: Any agreement reached through peacemaking has the effect of a court judgment when entered by the Tribal Court; peacemakers may decide a matter only with all parties' written consent.

facts.note: Requesting parties pay $25 each ($50 total) to the clerk for the Peacemaking Court. Proceedings are confidential and statements privileged. Crime victims are treated as parties for transfer purposes.

value.title: Traditional Peacemaking Court
value.citation: Sokaogon Chippewa Community Code, Chapter 1, Sections 1.1.8-1.1.12
value.summary: Establishes the Traditional Peacemaking Court, its jurisdiction, powers, confidentiality, fees, transfers from Tribal Court and juvenile jurisdiction.

value.name: Wodakota: Traditional Court

own_term.name: Wodakota
own_term.translation: The code describes the Wodakota way as the Dakota way of balance in dealings with oneself, the Creator and relatives; no single-word gloss is given.

value.description: Part of the Tribal Court system providing a non-adversarial, culturally appropriate mediation alternative to court-imposed sanctions; uses Peacemaking Circles drawing on elders, spiritual leaders and community members, and produces written peacemaking compacts.
value.legal_basis: Spirit Lake Law and Order Code, Title 21, §§ 21-1-101 to 21-1-110 and following
value.relationship_to_court: Cases may come informally, formally, by memorandum of agreement, or voluntarily; informal and formal matters remain under Tribal Court jurisdiction. All persons involved must consent through a memorandum of agreement. The court also offers peacemaking to community programs, schools and agencies under memoranda of agreement.
value.enforcement: A peacemaking compact signed by the parties and peacemaker becomes an order and judgment of the Tribal Court when the parties so intend and the Chief Judge signs it; peacemakers monitor compliance.

facts.note: The Title incorporates a tribal prayer adopted by elders, in English and Dakota, as a guideline (§ 21-1-105), and lists Dakota values with Dakota terms (§ 21-1-106); these are not reproduced here. Peacemaking Circles also serve as an alternative sentencing route for youth offenders. Language tag dak (Dakota).

value.name: Peacemaker System
value.description: Part of the Tribal Court System but independent from Tribal Court judges, giving formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Mohican methods of resolving disputes through mediation and traditional ways, under stated guiding principles including voluntary participation and community health.
value.legal_basis: Stockbridge-Munsee Tribal Code, Chapter TCT.04 (Peacemaker Ordinance), Sections TCT.04.01 to TCT.04.31
value.relationship_to_court: Civil actions may be referred by written stipulation of all parties and criminal matters on consent under listed conditions; a trial judge may also order parties in a civil case to spend at least one hour in a peacemaking session.
value.enforcement: Agreements may be confirmed as Tribal Court judgments and enforced as any other judgment; peacemakers may decide a matter only on all parties' written agreement (agreed arbitration).

facts.note: Peacemakers on the roll are tribal members over 35; parties may choose a non-member by agreement. Parties pay $20 each for peacemaker compensation. Attorneys barred except as witnesses or parties. as_of is NARF posting year.

value.title: Chapter TCT.04 – Peacemaker Ordinance
value.citation: Stockbridge-Munsee Tribal Code, Title TCT, Chapter TCT.04
value.summary: Establishes the Peacemaker System with guiding principles, peacemaker qualifications and powers, procedures, judgments, transfers and a one-hour mandatory civil peacemaking session option.

value.title: Ch’qi’n’txw an Offender’s Record of Conviction (Expungement)
value.citation: Lummi Nation Code of Laws, Title 5, Chapter 5.12 (5.12.010 and following)
value.summary: Lets a person who has completed all terms of a Lummi Tribal Court sentence petition to have the conviction ch’qi’n’txw, a term the code gives the same legal effect as expungement, grounded in the community value of forgiveness, with listed offenses excluded.

facts.note: A restorative, post-sentencing provision rather than a dispute forum; the code refers to living consistently with Lummi Sche’lang’en. Language tag str (Straits Salish) assigned on the basis that Lummi is a Northern Straits Salish language; the source does not name the language. Own term: ch’qi’n’txw.

value.name: Juvenile diversion conference with the Peacemaker coordinator
value.description: The Tribal prosecutor, with the concurrence of the juvenile probation officer and the Peacemaker coordinator, may divert a juvenile instead of filing a juvenile offender petition, holding an informal conference with the juvenile and parents or guardians on alternatives.
value.legal_basis: Grand Traverse Band Tribal Code, Title 10, Chapter 4, Sec. 415 (Diversion)
value.relationship_to_court: Occurs before a petition is filed; if positive results are not achieved after 30 days, the probation officer may recommend filing a petition.
value.enforcement: Conference findings and the agreed disposition are set out in writing and monitored by the juvenile probation officer; dispositions must conclude within six months unless extended by agreement; statements are inadmissible at a later trial.

facts.note: Parents or guardians must voluntarily consent after an explanation of rights; the prosecutor cannot compel involuntary action.

value.title: Juvenile Code – Diversion
value.citation: Grand Traverse Band Tribal Code, Title 10, Chapter 4, Sec. 415
value.summary: Authorizes pre-petition juvenile diversion conferences involving the prosecutor, juvenile probation officer and Peacemaker coordinator, with written agreed dispositions.

value.name: Peacemaking (Children's Court)

own_term.name: Odenaang Enjinoojimoying
own_term.translation: A Place of Healing Many Hearts (title of the Peacemaking Guidelines)

value.description: Peacemaking created in the Juvenile Code to provide a traditional conflict resolution process to children, youth and families, with a vision of resolution and healing.
value.legal_basis: Little River Band Juvenile Code (Ordinance #99-900-02), Sections 4.01(b), 4.02, 6, 7.01, 8
value.relationship_to_court: A juvenile's first status offense before the Children's Court is referred to the Peacemakers immediately; other cases come through the Case Intake Team (which includes a Peacemaker) or by Tribal Court referral, and cases go to court for adjudication if rejected or after nine months.

facts.note: Language tag otw assigned because the Band is Odawa (Ottawa); the code does not name the language. Participation recorded as court-referred because first status offenses are referred automatically by the code.

value.title: Juvenile Code – Peacemaking
value.citation: Little River Band Juvenile Code, Ordinance #99-900-02, Section 8
value.summary: Creates peacemaking for children, youth and families, directs the judiciary to issue Peacemaking Guidelines, and lists the cases peacemakers may hear.

value.title: Appendix 1 – Peacemaking Guidelines (Odenaang Enjinoojimoying), 2008

facts.note: NARF says the guidelines provide authorization, philosophical background, referral standards (including an option for traditional request), procedure, qualifications, standards of conduct, and forms.

value.name: Peacemaker Conference (Youth Code)
value.description: An informal conference in youth proceedings, which the code describes as an element of the Peacemaking Initiative, aimed at a written agreed disposition such as a Family Preservation Plan.
value.legal_basis: Jamestown S’Klallam Tribal Code, Title 33 – Youth Code, Section 33.01.16 and definition O
value.relationship_to_court: After a preliminary hearing any party may request a conference, or the Court may provisionally transfer a case on its own motion; if no agreement is reached, a fact-finding hearing is scheduled.
value.enforcement: A written agreement for a fixed period is signed by the child, parents or guardian, child advocate and the Tribe; the Indian Child Welfare Department monitors it and may recommend a fact-finding hearing for noncompliance.

facts.note: Kind recorded as family-or-talking-circle because it is a family-group conference within child welfare proceedings. Substantive information from the conference is inadmissible unless independently substantiated, except agreed Family Preservation Plan terms. The code's definition cites NARF's peacemaking site.

value.title: Peacemaker Conference
value.citation: Jamestown S’Klallam Tribal Code, Title 33, Section 33.01.16
value.summary: Provides for requesting, noticing and conducting Peacemaker Conferences in youth cases, written agreements, and monitoring of compliance.

value.name: Peacemaker Conference (Youth Code)
value.description: An informal conference in youth proceedings, conducted according to a process established by the Court, aimed at a written agreed disposition such as a Family Preservation Plan.
value.legal_basis: Nisqually Tribal Code, Title 50 – Youth, Sections 50.20.01 to 50.20.06
value.relationship_to_court: After a preliminary hearing any party may request a conference or the Court may provisionally transfer a case on its own motion; if no agreement is reached, a fact-finding hearing follows. Parties may also reach agreement outside a conference and present it to the Court.
value.enforcement: Written agreement for a fixed period signed by the child, parents or guardian, child advocate and the Tribe; Nisqually Children and Family Services monitors compliance; parties may present a draft order to formalize the agreement as a court order.

value.title: Peacemaker Conference
value.summary: Provides for Peacemaker Conferences in youth cases, with notice, informal procedure, written agreements, monitoring and formalization as court orders.

value.name: Youth Reclamation Program – The Peacemaker Program
value.description: A program to incorporate tribal culture and tradition in the Tribe's response to youth delinquency, using traditional peacemaking methods and restorative justice focused on restitution and healing; a Healing Circle develops a Healing Strategy that is supervised to completion.
value.legal_basis: Pit River Tribe, Title 8, Chapter 15, Sections 101-404 (under Article VI, sec. (1) of the Pit River Constitution)
value.relationship_to_court: An alternative to formal adjudication in tribal or state court; entry by petition of the prosecutor, child welfare coordinator or law enforcement, by application of family or community members, or by transfer from another jurisdiction with consent. Pending adjudication is stayed during participation.
value.enforcement: Failure to complete the program may lead to full prosecution or return of the child to the transferring jurisdiction; sanctions for non-compliance may be given.

facts.note: Peacemakers may be chosen by the tribal council, a court or judge, or elected by members; the clerk keeps a list.

value.title: Chapter 15 – Youth Reclamation Program – The Peacemaker Program
value.citation: Pit River Tribe, Title 8 Family/Children’s Code, Chapter 15
value.summary: Establishes a youth Peacemaker Program using Healing Circles and Healing Strategies as an alternative to adjudication.

value.name: Peacemaking Circle (White Earth juvenile justice)
value.description: A community-directed process in partnership with the tribal court for reaching consensus on a sentencing plan; the code describes circles as using traditional circle ritual and structure in which community members, elders, victims, the judge, attorneys, police and court workers speak in a shared search for understanding and healing.
value.legal_basis: White Earth Nation Juvenile Justice Code, Chapter 12A, Secs. 3-12-A-1 to 3-12-A-3; definition 30
value.relationship_to_court: After a guilty plea accepted by the Tribal Court judge, the court refers the offender to the juvenile counselor; the offender may choose not to participate, in which case the matter proceeds through adjudication or sentencing by the judge.
value.enforcement: The circle's consensus sentence agreement is presented to the judge for approval with information on meetings held and community involvement.

facts.note: White Earth is a component band of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe on the federal list; recorded under minnesota-chippewa-tribe with component_band. The offender and circle members create a social compact. as_of is NARF posting year. Component band: White Earth Band of Ojibwe.

value.title: Juvenile Justice Code, Chapter 12A – Peacemaking Circle (White Earth Nation)
value.citation: White Earth Nation Juvenile Justice Code, Chapter 12A
value.summary: Sets the application, scheduling and sentence agreement process for juvenile peacemaking circles after a guilty plea.

facts.note: Component band: White Earth Band of Ojibwe.

value.name: Peacemaking Circle (juvenile)
value.description: Per NARF, the Colville juvenile code provides for mandatory peacemaking referrals in both juvenile offender and child-in-need-of-care cases, with notice requirements, confidentiality and enforcement of disposition.
value.legal_basis: Colville Tribal Code, Title 5 Domestic Relations, Chapter 5-2 Juveniles, Sections 5-2-192 to 5-2-195 (Peacemaking Circle)
value.relationship_to_court: Referral from juvenile proceedings is mandatory per NARF's summary.

facts.note: NARF's linked PDF (Colville-Juvenile-Peacemaking-Circle-Code.pdf) returned 404 on 2026-11-21, so the code text was not read.

value.title: Juveniles – Peacemaking Circle
value.citation: Colville Tribal Code, Title 5, Chapter 5-2, §§ 5-2-192 to 5-2-195
value.summary: Per NARF, provides mandatory peacemaking referral for juvenile offender and child-in-need-of-care cases, notice, confidentiality and enforcement of disposition.

facts.note: Summary from NARF's description; code text not read (link returned 404).

value.title: Tribal Court Ordinance (peacemaking provisions)
value.citation: Grand Ronde Tribal Code, Chapter 302 (Tribal Court Ordinance), version dated 2013-10-23
value.summary: Per NARF, provides purpose, authorization and qualifications for peacemaking.

facts.note: NARF's linked PDF returned 404 on 2026-11-21; text not read.

value.name: Traditional Court
value.description: A court of Ho-Chunk elders for traditional dispute resolution within the Judiciary; per the Judiciary's page it provides knowledge of custom, traditions and Ho-Chunk core values to members referred by court processes, through social services programming, or by self-referral.
value.legal_basis: 1 HCC § 1 (Judiciary Establishment and Organization Act), Sections 3(c) and 13
value.relationship_to_court: Part of the Ho-Chunk Judiciary, established to assist the Judiciary whenever possible with cases or controversies involving Tribal members; a Traditional Court representative also sits on the Healing to Wellness Court and Family Wellness Court treatment teams.

facts.note: Case types are not enumerated in the sources reviewed. Referral routes are from the Judiciary's Traditional Court web page (accessed 2026-11-21).

value.title: Traditional Dispute Resolution
value.summary: Directs the Judiciary to provide for the establishment, operation and funding of the Traditional Court to assist with resolving cases involving Tribal members.

value.name: Mediation Services (Tulalip Tribal Court)
value.description: An out-of-court mediation process, conducted by Volunteers of America at the Tulalip Tribal Courthouse, in which a mediator helps disputants air the dispute and agree on a satisfactory solution.
value.relationship_to_court: Arranged through the Tribal Court main line; the page states a $400 fine for failing to appear without 48 hours' notice of cancellation.

facts.note: Participation recorded as court-referred because the page describes a no-show fine imposed through the court; the page does not state the legal basis. Case types not enumerated on the page; 'civil' reflects the description of disputants avoiding court.

value.name: Tribal Court Elders Panel
value.description: A culturally based program in which tribal elders volunteer on a panel that meets at the court every two weeks with young (18 to 25), first-time, non-violent offenders charged with minor offenses, favoring reparative over punitive justice.
value.relationship_to_court: Offenders volunteer; on completing one year of panel-imposed requirements their charges are dismissed in court.
value.enforcement: Requirements may include regular appearances, apology letters, community service, treatment, curfews, testing, family history research, spiritual activity, classes and evaluations; completion leads to dismissal.

value.name: Community Accountability Board (Juvenile Diversion Panel)
value.description: A volunteer community panel, operating since July 2010, that meets monthly with tribal member youths under 18 arrested for minor offenses to hold them accountable and increase awareness of their behavior.
value.relationship_to_court: A juvenile diversion program of the Tribal Court; meets at the Tribal Court.

facts.note: Participation as 'voluntary' is not stated explicitly; the page says eligible youth participate. Individual volunteer names on the page are not recorded.

value.title: Amendment to Tulalip Tribal Code 2.25, adding 2.25.200 enacting an Alternative Court Code (Resolution 2024-473)

facts.note: Known from a search result title only; the file returned 404 and contents were not read.

value.name: Native Justice Community Conflict and Dispute Resolution Forum
value.description: Native Justice, which the Band says is commonly referred to as peacemaking, uses talking circles and circle keepers to bring people in a dispute to common ground; circle keepers facilitate but do not decide, and participants set their own solution and consequences. The program has three strands: Native Justice for Court, the Community Conflict and Dispute Resolution Forum, and Community Education and Awareness.
value.relationship_to_court: Citizens may use the forum for civil disputes before coming to court; the court continues to handle criminal cases and encourages use of the forum for civil disputes.
value.enforcement: Participants design the consequences if standards they set are not met.

facts.note: The page says the process uses ceremonial traditions; no further detail is recorded.

value.title: Native Justice Resources (list of resources)

value.name: Mandatory Civil Mediation Program
value.description: An informal, flexible process in which a neutral mediator helps parties resolve their own disputes outside the adversarial process; the first step for all family-related civil cases filed in the Pascua Yaqui Tribal Court.
value.legal_basis: 5 PYTC Chapter 9 (Mediation), §§ 9-10, 9-30
value.relationship_to_court: The court clerk refers all civil cases involving families to mediation, for initial and modification proceedings; the court may decline referral on request for parental unfitness, substance abuse, mental incapacity, domestic violence, other good cause or undue delay, and a judge may refer a case at any time.

facts.note: Mandatory case types listed: marriage, dissolution of marriage, child custody and visitation, adoption, permanent guardianship or conservatorship, paternity, child support, probate.

value.title: Title 5 – Civil Code, Chapter 9 – Mediation
value.summary: Establishes the Mandatory Civil Mediation Program as the first step for family-related civil cases.

value.name: Peacemakers of the District Court (Kiowa Tribe Peacemaking Act)
value.description: The Act authorizes the District Court of the Kiowa Tribe to use peacemakers and provides for use of Kiowa Tribe traditions and customs, referral of existing actions, agreements and proposed orders, and enforcement of orders.
value.legal_basis: Kiowa Tribe Peacemaking Act, Sections 1-18

facts.note: Details from the Act's table of contents and opening section as quoted by NCORJ; the structure parallels the Choctaw Nation and Chickasaw Nation acts.

value.title: Kiowa Tribe Peacemaking Act

value.name: Wilton Rancheria Traditional Court
value.description: A division of the Tribal Court operating in accordance with the customs and traditions of the Tribe, providing a forum for traditional Wilton Rancheria methods of peacemaking to resolve disputes fairly, informally and inexpensively.
value.legal_basis: Wilton Rancheria Tribal Court Code, Chapter 1, Article V, §§ 1-501 to 1-509 (under Constitution Article VIII, Section 6); Rules of Procedure for the Traditional Court
value.relationship_to_court: The Chief Judge assigns cases to and supervises the Traditional Court and its members.

facts.note: NCORJ also lists separate Rules of Procedure for the Traditional Court.

value.title: Article V – Traditional Court
value.citation: Wilton Rancheria Tribal Court Code, Chapter 1, Article V, §§ 1-501 to 1-509

value.name: Traditional Conflict Resolution Program (TCRP)
value.description: A program to which the Tribal Court may refer cases; NCORJ classifies it as peacemaking and circle practice, and the Tribe's codes also refer elder and vulnerable adult protection matters and sentencing options to it.
value.legal_basis: Kenaitze Tribal Court Code, Sections 14(B), 17, 18; Domestic Relations Code, Chapter 10
value.relationship_to_court: At any time during a case the Court may refer it to the program if the judges find it appropriate; parties may request referral, and the presiding judges decide.

facts.note: Case types reflect the separate NCORJ records for Sections 14(B), 17 and 18 and Domestic Relations Code Chapter 10 (elder protection), which were listed but only Section 14(B) was read.

value.name: Forum for Traditional Dispute Resolution
value.description: The Court Administrator is directed to seek the assistance of Santee Sioux Nation elders to establish a traditional forum to provide guidance and assist the Judiciary with cases involving members.
value.legal_basis: Santee Sioux Nation Code, Title I, Chapter 1, Section 19
value.relationship_to_court: Assists the Judiciary whenever possible; a written report on its formation was due to the Tribal Council within twelve months of the Act.

facts.note: The provision directs establishment of the forum; whether it is operating was not verified.

value.name: Bekaadziiwiin (Peaceful Life) peacemaking

own_term.name: Bekaadziiwiin
own_term.translation: Peaceful Life (as given in the section heading)

value.description: A peacemaking diversion under guidelines promulgated by the Tribal Court; the Tribal Peacemaking Committee reviews cases presented by the Tribal Prosecutor and may decline action, refer to Bekaadziiwiin for peacemaking, develop a case plan, or refer to the Juvenile Division.
value.legal_basis: Sault Ste. Marie Tribal Code Chapter 36, § 36.405
value.relationship_to_court: Peacemakers may hear juvenile offenses, juvenile status offenses, other cases referred by the Tribal Court, and cases from tribal members who voluntarily request peacemaking; the Committee may ask the prosecutor to file a formal petition if a case plan is not substantially followed.

facts.note: The code spells the term both Bekaadziiwiin and Bekaadziiwin. Language tag oj (Ojibwe) assigned from the Tribe's identity; the source does not name the language.

value.name: Traditional Tlingit law in children's cases
value.description: Tribal Court judges may apply traditional Tlingit law by referring to written or oral accounts of traditional Tlingit life, interviewing Elders or Culture Bearers, or calling on the Haa Dachxanx’i Yan Jeeis (For Our Grandchildren) Committee or the Tribe's Cultural Resources Committee.

own_term.name: Haa Dachxanx’i Yan Jeeis
own_term.translation: For Our Grandchildren (committee name as glossed in the code)

value.legal_basis: Sitka Tribe Children's Code, Chapter VII, § 7.01
value.relationship_to_court: Traditional sources may give persuasive recommendations, but only the Presiding Judge enters a final order or judgment.

value.title: Problem Solving (alternative and traditional tools for dispute resolution)
value.summary: Allows the Presiding Judge to order alternative and traditional dispute resolution tools for all or part of a children's case, mindful of safety where there is evidence of domestic violence.

value.name: Associate Judges as Peacemakers
value.description: Elected Associate Judges act as peacemakers for the Tribal Court, attempting to resolve disputes through mediation and traditional peacemaking practices in cases involving at least one tribal member referred by the Chief Judge.
value.legal_basis: Habematolel Pomo Judicial Code, Chapter 1, Section 5.2(B)
value.relationship_to_court: Associate Judges may not make final decisions but may recommend settlement and resolution to the Chief Judge.

value.name: Peacemaking Panel and Peacemaker Program
value.description: A Peacemaking Panel that may mediate disputes at the parties' request before filing or as assigned by the Chief Judge after suit; the Peacemaker Program provides a nonadversarial way to resolve disputes, reflecting the Tribe's tradition of using respected community members to heal conflicts.
value.legal_basis: Grand Ronde Tribal Code Chapter 302 (Tribal Court Ordinance), Sections (c)(2)(A) and (l)
value.relationship_to_court: Parties are not precluded from filing or continuing a court claim if peacemaking is unsuccessful. Peacemakers are tribal members at least 25 years old approved by Tribal Council from the Chief Judge's list; they are volunteers.

facts.note: Combines NCORJ records for Chapter 302 sections (c)(2)(A) and (l). No party may be represented by counsel; a spokesperson may assist only as needed to understand the proceedings.

value.name: Family group conferencing / extended family hearing (juvenile)
value.description: Uses the extended families of the Community to help the juvenile court resolve juvenile offender, incorrigibility and dependency problems by applying the customs and traditions of the Pima and Maricopa peoples; the court may appoint a Community member qualified to act as a tribal elder to conduct the hearing.
value.legal_basis: Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community Code, § 11-31
value.relationship_to_court: The appointed elder makes written disposition recommendations to the court, which seeks to incorporate the extended family in its order.

value.name: Peacemaking Circle (custody and placement)
value.description: The court may refer a custody and placement case to the Peacemaking Circle when it believes the parties would benefit; the circle is completely voluntary and both parties must agree before transfer.
value.legal_basis: 4 HCC § 18 (Custody and Placement Ordinance), Section 9
value.relationship_to_court: The court must consider domestic abuse issues when deciding whether referral is appropriate.

value.name: Court-ordered mediation in child protection
value.description: After finding probable cause at a preliminary hearing the court may order custodians to participate in mediation; statements are not part of the record or used against them, except new abuse or neglect allegations, which are reported.
value.legal_basis: Waganakising Odawak Tribal Code of Law (WOTCL) 5.118(J)
value.relationship_to_court: Ordered by the court within child protection proceedings.

value.name: Peacemaking in child protection cases
value.description: In lieu of mediation, parties may request peacemaking, a voluntary and confidential process using cultural approaches to dispute resolution; statements cannot be used in court except new abuse or neglect allegations, which are reported.
value.legal_basis: Waganakising Odawak Tribal Code of Law (WOTCL) 5.118(K)
value.relationship_to_court: Available as an alternative to court-ordered mediation within child protection proceedings.

value.name: Peacemaking in child-in-need-of-care matters
value.description: The Child Welfare Director and affected parties (including a child 12 or older) may, by mutual consent, petition the Children's Court to institute peacemaking, conducted under rules set by peacemakers appointed by the Tribal Court.
value.legal_basis: LCO Code DMR.1.3.120 (Informal Disposition)
value.relationship_to_court: Occurs at the direction of the Children's Court; formal proceedings may be instituted at any time the Child Welfare Director deems appropriate.

value.name: Traditional Circle sessions (child support and paternity)
value.description: The domestic relations code refers to Traditional Circle sessions or stipulation conferences coordinated by the Child Support Program, in which in-kind support values may be stipulated.
value.legal_basis: Chippewa Cree Domestic Relations Code, Chapter 6 (Child Support), 6.6

facts.note: NCORJ also lists a related record on traditional circles for paternity cases. Participation recorded as voluntary because values are 'stipulated'; the excerpt does not otherwise state it.

value.name: Pueblo of Isleta Peacemaking Program
value.description: A permanent program within the Tribal Court, following a pilot project, giving parties a chance to resolve legal disputes informally with neutral peacemakers using traditional Pueblo methods of conflict resolution, and offering prevention and intervention sessions for at-risk youth.
value.legal_basis: Tribal Council Resolution No. 2020-028; Pueblo of Isleta Tribal Court Peacemaking Program Rules 1-6
value.relationship_to_court: Any dispute within the judicial branch's jurisdiction may be referred by agreement of the parties (signed request and court order) or by the court on its own initiative; pre-prosecution criminal referrals are allowed, but Major Crimes Act offenses are excluded. Two or more peacemakers are designated per case and no attorney or advocate may attend.
value.enforcement: A signed peacemaking agreement binds the parties; the court reviews it and either incorporates the settlement into a court order or returns the case to the docket. No appeal is allowed, but a party may move to enforce the agreement. Failure to attend may draw a fine of up to $100.

facts.note: Peacemakers must be enrolled members who understand Pueblo customs and traditions, are contracted by the Chief Judge with concurrence of sitting peacemakers, must complete peacemaker training, and are paid $25 per session hour. Statements are confidential and inadmissible.

value.title: Resolution Establishing Pueblo of Isleta Peacemaking Program and Peacemaking Program Rules
value.citation: Pueblo of Isleta Resolution No. 2020-028; Tribal Court Peacemaking Program Rules 1-6
value.summary: Makes the Tribal Court's peacemaking pilot permanent and sets rules on eligible cases, peacemaker qualifications and pay, referral, confidential sessions, binding agreements and enforcement.

value.name: Peacemaker training required before placement on the roster of trained peacemakers

facts.note: The rules require training and pay a flat fee for meeting or training attendance; the training curriculum is not described.

value.name: Keex’ Kwaan Peacemaking Court (Standing Peacemaking Panels and Peacemaking Circles)

own_term.name: Keex’ Kwaan
own_term.translation: Kake (the code uses it as the Tribe's own name for Kake, Alaska)

value.description: The Tribe's court, in which its judicial powers are vested, organized as peacemaking: a standing pool of at least twelve peacemakers (Council members and resident citizens) sitting in panels of three, Peacemaking Circles led by a Keeper of the Circle recognized by the Council, a Court of Appeals, and other courts the Council may create. The code applies written tribal laws and Keex’ Kwaan cultural values and traditions, and states that the ancestors formed the clan of Guwakaan, the Deer People, as the process of peacemaking, which no moiety claims.
value.legal_basis: Keex’ Kwaan Judicial Peacemaking Code, Chapter 1, Sections 1-12 (under Article V of the OVK Constitution)
value.relationship_to_court: The peacemaking court is the Tribe's judiciary; a review team of peacemakers decides whether to take a petition and whether to use a circle or a panel.
value.enforcement: Panels decide by consensus when possible and otherwise by majority vote; circles decide by consensus written as Consensus Agreements of the court, with set follow-up; if a circle cannot reach consensus the case goes to a panel.

facts.note: Read from OCR of a scanned copy. Peacemakers may consult Elders and Council members (Section 9). NARF notes the code includes a Peacemaker Appellate Court and a Circle Peacemaking flow chart. as_of is NARF posting year.

value.name: Kake Youth Circle Peacemaking (Kake Youth Community Restorative Peacemaking)
value.description: Part of the OVK Tribal Court system, encouraging responsible choices among youth, involving them in decisions about peers' problems, and producing Consensus Agreements designed to help and heal victims, wrongdoers and the Village; options include community service, restitution, apologies, essays, events, counseling by professionals, Elders or peers, talking circles and traditional activities.
value.legal_basis: Keex’ Kwaan Judicial Peacemaking Code, Chapter 4, Sections 1-13
value.relationship_to_court: Established by the OVK Council as part of the Tribal Court system, with a youth coordinator, youth panel and mentors.
value.enforcement: Consensus agreements with proof-of-compliance provisions and consequences for failure to comply (Section 12); appeals under Section 13.

facts.note: Participation recorded as court-referred because the chapter is part of the court system; voluntariness was not confirmed in the pages read.

value.title: Kake Peacemaking Handbook (2005)

value.name: Klamath Tribes Peacemaker Court
value.description: Part of the Tribal Court system providing a non-adversarial alternative using culturally appropriate mediation to reach conciliatory results rather than court-imposed sanctions, and giving formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Tribal methods of resolving disputes.
value.legal_basis: Klamath Tribal Code, Title 2, Chapter 18 (Klamath Peacemaker Ordinance), 18.01-18.15; Tribal Court Ordinance, Title 2, Chapter 11
value.relationship_to_court: Persons with a dispute, parties to any Tribal Court case, and juveniles in Tribal or state court Juvenile Matters are eligible; all parties must consent before transfer, and participation is entirely voluntary.
value.enforcement: A written Resolution signed by the parties and peacemaker becomes an order and judgment of the Tribal Court when the parties so intend and the Chief Judge signs it.

facts.note: Read from OCR. The court keeps a roster of at least three contracted peacemakers. Additional procedures for juvenile matters are in 18.12.

value.title: The Klamath Peacemaker Ordinance
value.summary: Establishes a voluntary Peacemaker Court with philosophy, peacemaker roster and qualifications, confidentiality, process, juvenile procedures and court entry of resolutions.

value.name: Peacemaker Tribunal (Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe Tribal Court)
value.description: A tribunal the Chief Judge may establish, as a permanent division or case by case, whose decisions bind the consenting parties; NARF associates the rule with the BaMeNim Anishinaabeg Program.

own_term.name: BaMeNim Anishinaabeg
own_term.translation: Program name as given by NARF; no gloss published in the sources reviewed.

value.legal_basis: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe Judicial Code, Title 2, Rules of Procedure, Rule 58
value.relationship_to_court: Use is voluntary and forecloses further use of the Trial Court except to enforce the tribunal's award or decision; parties must consent in writing and acknowledge they cannot appeal.
value.enforcement: Decisions are summarized in writing in the court file, are not appealable, and may be enforced through the Trial Court.

facts.note: Leech Lake is a component band of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe on the federal list. Kind recorded as arbitration because the rule describes a binding, non-appealable award or decision; the code calls it a Peacemaker Tribunal. Program name 'BaMeNim Anishinaabeg' comes from NARF's Tribal Peacemaking Laws page, not the rule itself. Component band: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe.

value.title: Rule 58: Peacemaker Tribunal
value.citation: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe Judicial Code, Title 2, Rule 58
value.summary: Authorizes the Chief Judge to create a voluntary Peacemaker Tribunal whose written, non-appealable decisions bind consenting parties.

facts.note: Component band: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe.

value.name: Peacemaker Court
value.description: Part of the judicial branch alongside the Tribal Court and Court of Appeals, with original jurisdiction over disputes involving minor civil matters between Snoqualmie tribal members and the application of tribal customs and traditions to tribal life.
value.legal_basis: Snoqualmie Judiciary Act 3.1, Sections 4.0, 5.0(c), 7.4
value.relationship_to_court: One of three components of the judicial branch; the section on the Peacemaker Court's operation (7.4) is marked Reserved in the copy reviewed.

facts.note: Read from OCR. The Act notes the Tribe contracts with the Northwest Intertribal Court System for judges. as_of is NARF posting year; whether the Peacemaker Court is operating was not verified.

value.name: Peacemaking program of the Tribal Court (guidelines)

own_term.name: Odenaang Enjinoojimoying
own_term.translation: A Place of Healing Many Hearts

value.description: Tribal Court peacemaking program for children, youth, adult tribal members and tribal employees; peacemakers guide the process, and participants develop and sign an agreement. A request may be made in the traditional way, by offering tobacco or another of the medicines named in the guidelines, or formally by court order or personal request.
value.legal_basis: Peacemaking Guidelines adopted by the Chief Judge and Associate Judge under the Juvenile Code
value.relationship_to_court: Cases may be referred by tribal courts, state courts, other federally recognized or historic tribes, or agencies, or come by personal request; cases the program declines go back to the Case Intake Team.
value.enforcement: The agreement is described as a binding contract; if participants do not follow it, the Tribal Court enforces it by court order.

facts.note: Read from OCR of a scanned document. 'employment' reflects the guidelines' eligibility of tribal employees; 'civil' reflects adult civil cases pending before the court. Language tag otw assigned because the Band is Odawa; the guidelines do not name the language.

value.name: Peacemaker certification (program operation, introduction to Anishinaabe culture, dispute resolution techniques; observation and a training session)

value.title: Odenaang Enjinoojimoying forms: intake (adult and youth), notice, peacemaking agreement, compliance, confidentiality agreement, follow-up questionnaire, community service log, contact log (appendices to the 2008 Guidelines)

value.name: Panel of elders in cultural causes of action
value.description: The Court of Central Jurisdiction enters as its judgment and order a decision made by a panel of elders in a cultural cause of action between Band members; the Court has jurisdiction over causes of action arising from unwritten cultural law.
value.relationship_to_court: Panel decisions are entered by the Court of Central Jurisdiction (the Chief Justice) as a judgment and order.
