value.enforcement: Entered as a court judgment and order; for cultural offenses the court may order sanctions consistent with Band traditions, including injunctions, removal, exclusion, community service or fines (24 MLBSA § 603).

facts.note: The statute text read does not say how a case reaches a panel of elders, how elders are chosen, or whether participation is voluntary, so participation is left out. 'Cultural harm' in 24 MLBSA § 602 concerns conduct that harms the community's good health or raises fear in the community; 'other' used for case type. Enforcement detail from Title 24 (source mille-lacs-title-24-judicial-proceedings). Component band: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe.

value.title: Cultural causes of action; panel of elders decisions
value.summary: Authorizes the Court of Central Jurisdiction to enter a panel of elders' decision in a cultural cause of action between Band members as a judgment and order.

facts.note: Component band: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe.

value.title: Cultural actions
value.summary: Gives any person a cause of action for cultural harm and lets the court impose sanctions consistent with Band traditions, such as injunctions, exclusion, community service or fines.

facts.note: Component band: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe.

value.name: Tribal youth court (youth wellness court program), Juneau
value.description: Planned opt-in program for youth tribal members in Southeast Alaska, described as an alternative to the regular justice system and built on tribal mentorship and tradition.

facts.note: News report of a program expected to launch within weeks; the launch is not confirmed in the source. Read through a fetch-and-summarize tool.

value.name: Village authority over family disputes
value.description: The Constitution reserves to each village the power to adjust family disputes and regulate family relations of village members, along with appointing guardians, regulating inheritance and assigning farming land; each village decides how it is organized, and a village that has not chosen another form is considered to be under traditional Hopi organization.
value.legal_basis: Constitution of the Hopi Tribe, Article III, Sections 2-3
value.relationship_to_court: A power reserved to the villages, separate from the courts the Tribal Council may set up under Article VI.

facts.note: The Constitution states the reserved powers; it does not describe how individual villages carry them out, so no procedure, participation or enforcement is recorded.

value.name: Tribal Council hearing of disputes between villages
value.description: When villages dispute any matter, the Kikmongwi of a village party may ask the Chairman to call a special Council meeting; the Council hears representatives and witnesses, decides in a closed meeting by majority vote, and keeps a record of the evidence and its reasons.
value.legal_basis: Constitution of the Hopi Tribe, Article VIII
value.enforcement: A village party that considers the decision unjust may, within ten days, seek review by the Secretary of the Interior.

facts.note: Participation recorded as voluntary because the text says a village party 'may' ask for the meeting. Secretarial review is as stated in the constitution text read.

value.title: Powers reserved to the villages
value.summary: Reserves to the individual villages the powers to appoint guardians, adjust family disputes, regulate inheritance and assign farming land.

value.title: Disputes Between Villages
value.summary: Sets a Tribal Council hearing and decision procedure for disputes between villages, with review by the Secretary of the Interior on a village's request.

Makes written agreements to arbitrate contract claims valid and enforceable in Tribal Court, with no appeal from orders enforcing an agreement or award, and creates a Tribal Commercial Court division to hear matters under the Arbitration Code and the Tribal Uniform Commercial Code.

A Band contract to arbitrate must be approved by a Tribal Council resolution specifically waiving immunity to arbitrate, to have the agreement enforced and to have the award enforced; the Council may by resolution waive Tribal Court jurisdiction or give another venue priority.

value.citation: 7 PYTC §§ 6-10 to 6-150 (Business and Commercial Code, Arbitration Ordinance)
value.summary: Makes written agreements to arbitrate enforceable, gives the Tribal Court jurisdiction to compel arbitration and confirm awards (no appeal from awards), and allows actions against the Tribe or its entities only where the contract explicitly waives immunity; the ordinance itself waives no immunity.

value.citation: Jamestown S'Klallam Tribal Code, Title 2 (Arbitration Code), Sections 2.01.02, 2.02.01-2.02.08
value.summary: Makes written agreements to arbitrate enforceable, provides for Tribal Court confirmation of awards with no appeal, and gives the Tribal Court jurisdiction over actions involving the Tribe only where the Tribal Council has granted a limited waiver of immunity under the Tribe's waiver code.

Makes written agreements to arbitrate enforceable, provides for confirmation of awards by the Tribal Forum with no appeal, and allows actions against the Nation or its entities only where the instrument explicitly waives immunity; the ordinance itself waives no immunity.

value.citation: LCO Tribal Code of Law TCT.1.3.030
value.summary: Allows limited waivers of immunity only by express Tribal Governing Board resolution or motion, including a waiver in an employment agreement to enforce its terms in tribal court, and requires each waiver to be specific as to duration, grantee, transaction, assets, court and applicable law.

facts.note: Context: Sovereign immunity code; waiver may be granted in employment agreements.

value.summary: Bars officials and employees of the Tribe or its enterprises from signing a contract containing a sovereign immunity waiver without a separate resolution authorizing the waiver.

facts.note: Codified in Title 7 (Contracts), Chapter 7.07 (Unlawful Contract Provisions). The published text begins mid-sentence.

value.name: Court of Elders
value.description: A body of two to six citizens of the Tlingit & Haida communities, including elder village tribal citizens, appointed for a particular matter to resolve disputes by traditional methods and answer questions of customary law. It gives written advisory opinions on questions certified by the Tribal Court and, on the parties' joint written request, may hear and mediate disputes among citizens using traditional law and custom; it may seek advice from sources knowledgeable on Tlingit and Haida clan custom.
value.legal_basis: Title 06 Tribal Courts, Chapter 04 (Secs. 06.04.001-06.04.004); Sec. 06.01.003(I)
value.relationship_to_court: Part of the judicial system with the Supreme Court and Trial Court; the Tribal Court certifies customary-law questions to it, and it hears only disputes not governed by tribal law and not otherwise within the Tribal Court's jurisdiction. No attorneys or lay advocates.
value.enforcement: Its written decision or agreement is filed by the Tribal Court Clerk and treated as a final judgment, with no appeal.

facts.note: Members are appointed by the President of Tlingit & Haida; no names recorded. Case types not listed in the code, so 'other' is used.

value.title: Court of Elders
value.summary: Sets up a Court of Elders that issues advisory opinions on customary law certified by the Tribal Court and may, by joint consent, mediate disputes among citizens, with its decisions filed as final, unappealable judgments.

value.name: Panel of Elders
value.description: Twelve elders appointed by the Tribal Council (four from each district) advise the Tribal Court on disputes under White Earth law when a party asks; the Chief Judge presides and assigns one elder to advise in each case. Elders may also serve as jurors, one may sit on the Appellate Panel, and a Band member, including a juvenile, may choose to have a case heard in consultation with an elder in accordance with the Band's traditional values and practices.
value.legal_basis: White Earth Judicial Code, Title 1, Chapter VIII (Sections 1-7); Chapter I Section 1; Chapter VII Section 6(b)
value.relationship_to_court: Part of the White Earth Tribal Court; advises the court on request, and the court may also seek the panel's advice when custom or tradition is in doubt.

facts.locator: Chapter I § 1; Chapter III § 6; Chapter VII § 6(b); Chapter VIII §§ 1-7
facts.note: Read by OCR. The chapter applies to all actions within the court's jurisdiction; only juveniles are named expressly, so other case types are recorded as 'other'. The panel may adopt its own rules of procedure. as_of is the scan date because no enactment date was found. Component band: White Earth Band of Ojibwe.

value.title: Panel of Elders
value.citation: White Earth Judicial Code, Title 1, Chapter VIII
value.summary: Creates a twelve-member Panel of Elders that advises the court on request of a party, may serve on juries and the Appellate Panel, and sets its own procedure.

facts.note: Read by OCR; enactment date not found. Component band: White Earth Band of Ojibwe.

value.title: Distribution of Traditional and Cultural Items
value.summary: Lets next of kin distribute a decedent's artifacts and finery according to Band custom, with the Tribal Court resolving disputes with the advice of traditional elders from the decedent's community when possible.

facts.note: Section number as shown in the text read; chapter not confirmed. Component band: White Earth Band of Ojibwe.

value.citation: White Earth Tribal Housing Ordinance, Article IX
value.summary: Gives the Housing Authority power to sue and to agree to arbitration.

facts.note: Scanned text with OCR errors; meaning read from the garbled text layer. Component band: White Earth Band of Ojibwe. Context: Tribal housing ordinance (Housing Authority powers).

value.citation: White Earth Tribal Housing Ordinance, Article IX
value.summary: Lets the Housing Authority grant limited waivers of its immunity and consent to suit in the White Earth Tribal Court, without waiving the Tribe's immunity and with recovery limited to Housing Authority assets.

value.summary: Waives immunity of the utilities Commission and its Executive Director only for Tribal Court review of their final decisions, limited to prospective equitable relief and excluding money damages.

facts.note: Component band: White Earth Band of Ojibwe. Context: Utilities code (regulatory commission review).

value.name: Peacemaking (Tribal Court)
value.description: The Tribal Court uses peacemaking to mediate cases where dispute resolution is preferred over an adversarial approach; the Honoring Nations report says it has helped resolve contentious issues while keeping community ties. The court's current staff list includes a peacemaker and program director position.
value.relationship_to_court: Used by the Tribal Court as part of its handling of disputes.

facts.note: Secondary source (Honoring Nations 1999 report). The staff position is from the Band's Tribal Court web page (https://gtbindians.org/tribal_court.asp, read 2026-11-21); no staff names recorded. Case types for peacemaking are not stated, so none are recorded.

value.summary: Employment issues other than the enumerated employee rights must go through the internal dispute resolution process, which may be a grievance process or an employee mediation panel under the Employment Manual, and that process must be exhausted before a Tribal Court appeal.
Provides a limited waiver of immunity for timely claims under the enumerated employee rights, limited to the non-monetary remedies listed in the ordinance such as reinstatement.

value.title: Employee Rights Ordinance – peacemaking for employee disputes
value.summary: Permits peacemaking for employee disputes, to be conducted under the Tribal Peacemaker Ordinance.

value.name: Mnodaawin Peacemaking Circles (juvenile)
value.description: Tribal Court alternative to the usual judicial process, first offered for juvenile cases such as truancy, curfew, incorrigibility and minor offenses. Trained facilitators lead circles of the juvenile, parents, family, elders and community members (the victim may take part or be represented) until they reach a written consensus agreement signed by all, followed by monitoring circles over several months. The page says the Tribal Court plans similar processes for civil disputes.
value.relationship_to_court: Used in place of going before the judge; available only where the juvenile admits wrongdoing and the juvenile and a parent or guardian agree.
value.enforcement: Follow-up circles over several months monitor compliance with the signed agreement.

facts.note: Official page but undated (as_of is the access date), so confidence is low under the contract; it reads as a program description from the program's start. Agreements may include school, community service, cultural activities, counseling and restitution commitments. Contact person on the page not recorded.

value.name: Peacemakers Court (brochure description)
value.description: The brochure lists ideal cases as family disputes (spouses, parents and children, extended families), community disputes (nuisance, trespass, disorderly conduct, disturbing the peace), financial disputes (personal debts, breach of contract) and individual land-use and access disputes. Sessions include one male and one female peacemaker, no lawyers, voluntary participation, and a binding resolution agreed by all parties. Guiding principles are given in English and Wampanoag.
value.relationship_to_court: Part of the Tribal Judiciary; the Chief Judge of the Supreme Court supervises the Peacemakers Court and the appointed peacemakers.
value.enforcement: The final decision is agreed upon by all parties and described as binding.

facts.note: The numeral 8 is part of the Wampanoag spelling as printed and is kept exactly. Language tag wam (Wampanoag) assigned because the brochure gives Wampanoag terms beside English; the brochure does not name the language. Supervision detail from the Tribe's About Peacemakers Court page. Peacemaker names printed in the brochure are not recorded.

log.limits: Coverage is uneven by design: depth comes from codes on the NARF Indigenous Peacemaking Initiative pages and from nations' own sites; breadth comes from two bulk sources. (1) 940 NCORJ Restorative Justice Tribal Laws Database records were turned into dispute-resolution-provision facts automatically; they were not reviewed one by one, their kind is assigned from NCORJ's taxonomy, and many concern restorative sentencing, diversion or treatment rather than ADR as such. (2) 131 facts come only from section titles in National Indian Law Library tables of contents; the provision text was not read, so they have no summary and their kind is assigned from words in the title (watch for 'other' = generic 'dispute resolution' sections, many in gaming, workers' compensation and labor codes). Two NARF-linked PDFs returned 404 (Colville juvenile peacemaking circle code, Grand Ronde tribal court ordinance 2013), so those facts rest on NARF's summaries. Several codes were scanned images read by OCR (Isleta, Kake, Klamath, Leech Lake, Little River guidelines, Oneida NY rules, Snoqualmie, White Earth Judicial Code) and the Hopi constitution and White Earth housing ordinance have poor text layers; OCR errors are possible. Mille Lacs Titles 5 and 24, the Grand Traverse NNI page, the KTOO Tlingit & Haida article and the NJC Pechanga article were read through a fetch-and-summarize tool because direct download failed or for speed. Tulalip's code moved to ecode360, which blocked fetching, so the Tulalip Alternative Court Code (Resolution 2024-473) is recorded from a search result only (low). ecode360, yurok.tribal.codes and karuk.tribal.codes returned 403; the Pechanga site reset connections; the Ponca (Nebraska) code PDF and the Northern Arapaho code page returned 404. Navajo brochure and referral form links are search-only (low). No specific peacemaking or ADR program was found for Muscogee (Creek) Nation, Cherokee Nation (beyond NILL section titles and NCORJ records), or Puyallup after two or more searches each; that means not found, not none. No NAICJA or BJS survey tables were used (no per-nation ADR data located in time). No state-recognized nation with a documented ADR practice was found, so no entities were added. Undated official web pages are marked low confidence per the contract even when they come from the nation itself. Minnesota Chippewa Tribe component bands (Leech Lake, White Earth, Mille Lacs) are recorded under minnesota-chippewa-tribe with value.component_band. Extra value keys used beyond the contract: own_term {name, language_tag, romanized, translation}, component_band, context_detail, title_as_listed, and NCORJ taxonomy keys on bulk records. Language tags were assigned where the source gives a Native-language term but does not name the language (each such case is explained in the fact note); 'und' is used where the language could not be identified from the source.
log.narrative: Method: (1) Downloaded every code, rule and guide linked from the three NARF Indigenous Peacemaking Initiative model-law pages, extracted text (OCR for scans), and wrote curated forum, provision, material and training facts for each nation, recording Native-language names exactly as printed (for example Nanna alphi’sa ishtaa-asha ikbi, Itti-kāna-ikbi, Gwe-shvt-naga, Wodakota, Mnodaawin, Odenaang Enjinoojimoying, Bekaadziiwiin, Keex’ Kwaan, Haa Dachxanx’i Yan Jeeis, Wunahtyâhe8âôk, hózh̨óji naat’aah). (2) Pulled all 940 NCORJ tribal-law records through the site's REST API, scraped the tribe name from each record page, matched names to roster ids, and turned each record into a provision fact; about 20 records describing distinct programs were also written up as curated forum facts. (3) Read nations' own court pages and codes for nations named as priorities and for the strongest leads (Navajo, Tulalip, Ho-Chunk, Grand Traverse, Little Traverse, Little River, Mille Lacs, White Earth, Hopi, Tlingit & Haida, Siletz, Mashpee, Choctaw nations), upgrading confidence where the nation publishes the same or a newer text. (4) For clauses, read tribal arbitration ordinances and sovereign-immunity waiver sections in commercial, employment, housing and utilities codes (Little River, Pascua Yaqui, Jamestown S'Klallam, Ho-Chunk, Lac Courte Oreilles, Turtle Mountain, Stockbridge-Munsee, White Earth) and added Little Traverse loan statutes whose titles adopt arbitration law. Gaming compacts were left to the gaming helper. (5) Added training facts from NARF news posts and the Little River and Isleta rules. (6) Scanned all NILL tribal code tables of contents for dispute-resolution words to add breadth. The model keeps forum kinds open: besides the suggested values it records an employment tribunal (Prairie Band Potawatomi), village-reserved family dispute authority and a council hearing of inter-village disputes (Hopi), a Court of Elders that mediates by joint consent (Tlingit & Haida), elders panels that advise courts (White Earth, Mille Lacs, Tulalip), agreed arbitration by peacemakers (Siletz, Chitimacha, Northern Arapaho), settlement conferences, and family group conferencing.
